heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Cherry types are heat resistant, so this pause is shorter for them than for large-fruited tomatoes, and a few varieties keep setting through it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). Unlike the milder southeastern summer, this desert pause is climatic-absolute: it is wide and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance, because even heat-tolerant cherry types cannot set fruit in extreme desert summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by cherry's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

value.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for cherry tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Cherry types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit-set failure is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Large-fruited beefsteak is more heat-sensitive than cherry types (which are heat resistant), so its summer pause is wider, running across June through August rather than the single midsummer month a cherry holds. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

The low desert summer is a climatic-absolute fruit-set exclusion: extreme day and night temperatures cause complete blossom drop from June through August for every tomato type. Large-fruited beefsteak is at least as heat-sensitive as cherry, so this Jun-Aug pause is not narrowed (it cannot be shortened the way a marginal-zone pause can). (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC IPM)

The Maricopa low-desert summer is a fruit-set exclusion from June through August: extreme day and night temperatures cause complete blossom drop. AZ1005 marks no tomato transplant from late spring through midsummer. Large-fruited beefsteak fails earlier than cherry here, so the pause runs the full June-August rather than cherry's July-August. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1005)

value.calendar_basis: Beefsteak tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This desert pause is climatic-absolute and wide: peak desert summer heat stops fruit set for roma as for any large-fruited tomato. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by extra heat tolerance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Bell pepper drops its blossoms and sets little fruit through the hot, humid heart of a Gulf and Florida summer, when daytime highs above about 90°F combine with warm, muggy nights above the mid-70s°F. Peppers here are grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, with midsummer paused for poor fruit set, a lull compounded by heavy disease and pest pressure. The pause reflects heat-driven blossom drop, not cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional pattern.

Bell pepper sets fruit poorly in extreme heat: when daytime highs climb past about 90 to 95°F and nights stay warm, the flowers drop instead of setting, and exposed fruit sunscalds. In the low desert, July and August highs well into the 100s°F halt fruit set, so desert growers run a late-winter-to-spring crop that finishes before peak heat and a second crop set out in September as the heat eases, leaving midsummer paused. The pause reflects heat-driven blossom drop, not cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

Bell pepper sets fruit poorly in extreme heat: when daytime highs climb past about 90 to 95°F and nights stay warm, the flowers drop instead of setting, and exposed fruit sunscalds. In the low desert, July and August highs well into the 100s°F halt fruit set, so desert growers run a late-winter-to-spring crop that finishes before peak heat and a second crop set out in September as the heat eases, leaving midsummer paused. The pause reflects heat-driven blossom drop, not cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit when daytime highs pass about 90°F and, especially, when nighttime lows stay above 75°F, which UMD notes will slow or stop pod production. Across the Gulf and coastal plain, July and August bring exactly that combination of heat and warm nights (compounded by humidity and disease pressure), so fruit set pauses through the peak of summer. Growers therefore run a spring crop that sets before the heat and a fall crop as it eases, leaving midsummer paused. This pause reflects reduced fruit set at high temperature, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit above about 90°F days and 75°F nights (NMSU notes chile blossoms may fail to set above 90°F). In the California desert valleys, June through August routinely exceed 105 to 110°F by day with nights well above 75°F, far past the threshold, so even a well-watered pepper sets no fruit through those months. Desert growers run a late-winter planting for a late-spring crop and a September planting for a fall and early-winter crop, leaving the deep-summer weeks paused. This pause reflects blocked fruit set at extreme heat, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

Like tomato, jalapeno drops its blossoms and stops setting fruit above about 90°F days and 75°F nights (NMSU notes chile blossoms may fail to set above 90°F). Arizona's low desert routinely exceeds 105 to 110°F from June through August with warm nights, far past the threshold, so fruit set stops through those months. Low-desert growers plant in February for a late-spring crop and again in late summer for a fall crop, leaving the deep-summer weeks paused. This pause reflects blocked fruit set at extreme heat, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

The summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in deep-summer heat slicing-cucumber flowering and fruit set falter and the fruit turns bitter. When daytime highs run in the 90s°F and higher with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and pollen so plants set poorly or drop young fruit, and heat-plus-drought stress drives the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) into what fruit does form. Set and quality recover as temperatures ease, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (regional extension planting chart; UMN Extension growing cucumbers)

value.zone_notes: A long cool-season window: plant from late summer into fall, harvest through a mild winter into spring. Summer is too hot.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: kale is a cool-season brassica that grows and tastes best when average temperatures stay around 55°F to 75°F. Through the hot months its leaves turn tough and bitter, plants are prone to bolting (running to flower), and pressure from aphids and harlequin bugs peaks, so kale is grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the summer is left out of the planting calendar. Along the warm Gulf coast kale is a fall-through-spring crop; summer heat and humidity make poor, buggy leaves. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; LSU AgCenter)

value.zone_notes: A long fall-through-spring window with mild winter harvest; the warmest midsummer weeks are the gap, though coastal plantings can sometimes run through summer.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: kale is a cool-season brassica that grows and tastes best when average temperatures stay around 55°F to 75°F. Through the hot months its leaves turn tough and bitter, plants are prone to bolting (running to flower), and pressure from aphids and harlequin bugs peaks, so kale is grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the summer is left out of the planting calendar. Inland south-coast summers warm enough to turn kale bitter and bolt-prone, so midsummer is left out; right at the coast it can be pushed through summer with some bitterness. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Master Gardeners San Diego County)

value.zone_notes: Warm coastal zone 9: the productive window is the cool fall through spring, with a long winter harvest, and only a brief early-spring sowing. The hot season stretches May through August, when spinach bolts and will not germinate.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Spinach is a cool-season crop that grows best when temperatures stay below about 75°F, and its seed germinates poorly above 75 to 85°F. Through the hot months of the lower coastal plain it bolts almost at once under long days and high heat, the leaves turn bitter, and new sowings fail to establish, so spinach is grown here as a fall-through-spring crop and the summer is left out of the planting calendar.

value.zone_notes: The warmest south-coast zone grows spinach in the cool fall, winter, and spring; summer heat excludes it. Coastal microclimates can sometimes push it later, but inland heat bolts it by June.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for sugar snap peas, not a frost gap. value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 300 chill hours most winters, below even Florida King's roughly 400-hour requirement. value.type_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is gated in by your moderate chill (about 350 to 650 hours) and long, hot summers. It is native to the region, the most heat-tolerant type, and blooms late enough to dodge most spring freezes; northern highbush gets too little chill here and resents the summer heat.
value.type_note_beginner: Rabbiteye is the type that loves the warm Southeast. Your winters are not cold enough for northern types, but they are just cold enough for rabbiteye, which also handles the summer heat and flowers late enough to usually avoid frost damage.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye blooms later than southern highbush and usually escapes spring freezes, but a warm late-winter spell can push bloom early, and a hard freeze on open flowers can cut the crop sharply. Later-blooming cultivars are the safer bet.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Rabbiteye is a permanent evergreen shrub in the Gulf South, planted once and productive for decades; it holds its leaves through the mild winter and stays in leaf year round. The year runs from a late, frost-dodging bloom to harvest from roughly late May into July, then a quieter care period of light shaping and feeding. Rabbiteye needs a second, different rabbiteye nearby to cross-pollinate and set a crop.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Your rabbiteye blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years, and here it stays green all year. It flowers late enough to usually miss spring frosts, ripens berries from late spring into summer, then moves into a calmer stretch of light tidying and feeding. One key point: it must have a second, different rabbiteye variety planted nearby so the two can pollinate each other and make fruit.

value.type_note_seasoned: Very-low-chill southern highbush is the match for the mild southern coast, where winters rarely deliver much cold; it is grown as an evergreen here. Very-low-chill rabbiteye is a fallback where chill is especially scarce.
value.type_note_beginner: Southern highbush varieties with very low chill needs are the right choice on the mild southern California coast, because winters here barely get cold. They tend to keep their leaves year-round in this gentle climate.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is seldom a problem on the southern coast; very-low-chill types bloom early, so an inland late frost can occasionally nip open bloom, but summer heat and dry air are the bigger stresses.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Southern highbush grows as a permanent evergreen on the mild southern coast, planted once and productive for decades; it keeps its leaves year round. The year runs from a late-winter bloom to harvest from roughly late May into August, then a care period of light shaping and feeding. Heat and dry air, not frost, are the main stresses, so give afternoon shade in hot spots.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Your southern highbush blueberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for many years, and on the mild coast it stays green all year. It flowers in late winter, ripens berries from late spring into late summer, then settles into a calmer stretch of light care and feeding. The bush handles cold easily here; it is summer heat you watch for, so give it afternoon shade where the sun is strong.

value.type_note_seasoned: Only very-low-chill southern highbush has a chance in the desert, and only in containers; even then chill is marginal. It is the lowest-chill, most heat-leaning type, grown evergreen here.
value.type_note_beginner: If any blueberry can grow in the desert, it is a very-low-chill southern highbush, and only in a pot. These need the least winter cold of all the types, which matters where winters are warm.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limiting factor in the low desert; extreme summer heat on developing fruit and marginal winter chill are the real constraints, so the harvest finishes early before peak heat.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the California low desert blueberry is a container-only crop, since native soils are too alkaline for it; grown that way it is a permanent evergreen shrub that holds its leaves year round. The year runs from an early bloom to an early harvest, April into May before peak heat, then a care period of light shaping, feeding, and steady acidic watering. Give afternoon shade and treat it as a rewarding challenge rather than a sure thing.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the California desert, blueberries only work in large pots because the ground soil is too alkaline. Grown that way it is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years, staying green all year. It flowers early and ripens berries in spring, around April to May, before the worst heat, then moves into a calmer stretch of light care and careful watering. Give it afternoon shade against the intense sun, and know this is a project for a patient gardener.

value.type_note_seasoned: Only very-low-chill southern highbush is viable, in containers, and it performs best at mid-elevation rather than the low desert; chill in the low desert is marginal even for this type.
value.type_note_beginner: The only blueberry worth trying in the low desert is a very-low-chill southern highbush, grown in a container. It needs the least winter cold of any type, but even so the low desert is a stretch.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the limiting factor in the low desert; alkaline soil, extreme summer heat, and marginal winter chill are the binding constraints, so an early harvest finishes before peak heat.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert blueberry is a container-only crop, since the soil is too alkaline for in-ground planting; grown in pots it is a permanent evergreen shrub that keeps its leaves year round. The year runs from a mid-winter bloom to an early harvest, April into May, then a care period of light shaping, feeding, and acidified watering. Shield it from extreme heat; it performs best in cooler mid-elevation spots.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Around the Arizona low desert, blueberries have to be grown in large containers because the ground soil is too alkaline. Grown that way it is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years, staying green all year. It flowers in mid-winter and ripens berries in spring, around April to May, then settles into a calmer stretch of light care and careful watering. Protect it from the harshest heat, and expect better results in the cooler mid-elevation areas.

value.type_note_seasoned: Only low-chill and no-chill southern highbush cultivars fruit in Hawaii, grown evergreen and usually in containers at 250 to 4000 feet. Northern highbush and rabbiteye are not suited to the islands' chill.
value.type_note_beginner: In Hawaii, only the lowest-chill southern highbush varieties will fruit, since there is essentially no winter cold. They are grown in containers and stay green all year.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor in Hawaii. During bloom and fruiting the practical concerns are choosing genuinely low-chill or no-chill cultivars and managing blueberry rust in cool, wet, high-elevation sites.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In Hawaii blueberry is a niche, long-lived evergreen crop, planted once and kept for years, grown almost always in containers from roughly 250 to 4000 feet; only low-chill and no-chill southern highbush fruit here, and they hold their leaves year round. The year runs from bloom to harvest, then a care period of light shaping and feeding, the bush staying in leaf the whole time. Watch for blueberry rust in cool, wet sites, and treat it as a rewarding specialty.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In Hawaii, blueberries are a fun specialty crop you plant once and keep for years, grown almost always in pots with special low-chill or no-chill varieties, and the bush stays green all year. It flowers, ripens its berries, then settles into a calmer stretch of light care and feeding, staying in leaf the whole time. Keep an eye out for a leaf disease called rust in cool, damp spots, and enjoy it as something a little out of the ordinary.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer fruit set fails from heat, not frost: like all tomatoes, heirloom flowers abort and drop once daytime highs pass the upper 80s to 90s°F and nights stay above about 70°F, when pollen turns non-viable. Large-fruited heirlooms are as heat-sensitive as any large tomato, so Jun through Aug is a set-failure window rather than a growing gap. (Penn State Extension, Heat Stress and Tomatoes; University of Missouri IPM, Understanding Tomato Fruit Set)

value.calendar_basis: Heirloom tomato can be planted YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no documented summer no-sow exclusion: CTAHR HGV-5 states tomato can be grown throughout the year in most places in Hawaii by choosing adapted varieties, and names no seasonal fruit-set gap. UNLIKE cherry (which CTAHR treats as cleanly heat resistant), CTAHR's Field Tomato Production Guidelines specifically warn that large-fruited varieties set fruit poorly under Hawaii's warm lowland nights (optimum fruit set 60-70 deg-F). This is a fruit-set-QUALITY caveat, disclosed in the seasoned region_note, not an absolute no-sow month, so the year-round structure holds (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted; HGV-5 documents no exclusion month). Hawaii's dominant challenge is disease, insect, and heavy-rain pressure, managed with resistant locally bred cultivars (Kewalo, Anahu, Healani, N-series) and cultural practice. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason; year_round:true makes the all-active calendar machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR HGV-5; CTAHR Field Tomato Production Guidelines for Hawaii)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: high day and especially night temperatures push tomato flowers to drop and fruit set to fail. Grape types are heat resistant, so this pause is shorter for them than for large-fruited tomatoes, and a few varieties keep setting through it. (UGA Cooperative Extension C943; UF/IFAS VH021)

The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run well past 95°F and often above 110°F, and tomato flowers fail to set fruit once temperatures stay above about 95°F (high heat reduces viable pollen). Unlike the milder southeastern summer, this desert pause is climatic-absolute: it is wide and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance, because even heat-tolerant grape types cannot set fruit in extreme desert summer heat. (UC ANR Master Gardener Handbook Table 13.2; UC Statewide IPM Program)

The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, poor fruit development is expected through the peak of summer (July and August), because daytime temperatures above 90°F reduce the number of viable pollen grains and stop fruit set. The main spring crop runs from a mid-March transplant through late June, then the July-August peak halts set; planting resumes in September once the heat passes. As in the California desert, this pause is climatic-absolute and is not narrowed by grape's heat resistance. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension az2078)

value.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for grape tomato: CTAHR gives tomato a year-round planting capability for most of Hawaii, contingent on adapted varieties. The limiting factors are disease (tomato spotted wilt and tobacco mosaic viruses, and warm-wet leaf spots and blights), insect pests (whitefly, leafminer, fruit fly, thrips), and fruit cracking in heavy rain, managed with resistant locally-bred UH cultivars, staking or caging to keep fruit off the ground, morning soil-only irrigation, and successive plantings, rather than by pausing a season. Grape types and the compact determinates (for example 'Healani') also do well in 3 to 5 gallon containers here.

This is the per-region source finding: the grape summer heat_pause documented for the Florida peninsula and the deserts does not universalize to Hawaii's oceanic lowland (guardrail: heat_pause is read from the source per region, never defaulted). heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Banana pepper, like all peppers, drops its blossoms and sets little fruit through the hot, humid heart of a Gulf, Florida, or desert summer, when daytime highs above about 90°F combine with warm nights above the mid-70s°F. Peppers here are grown as a spring crop and a fall crop, with midsummer paused for poor fruit set, a lull compounded in the humid South by heavy disease and pest pressure. The pause reflects heat-driven blossom drop, not cold, and is grounded in pepper-specific heat thresholds rather than a tomato source. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional pattern.

The deep-Gulf midsummer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the warmest coastal zone, July and August bring sustained days above 90°F and humid nights above 75°F, and pepper flowers drop and pod set stalls under those conditions (Maryland extension: evening temperatures above 75°F slow or stop pepper pod production). Cayenne tolerates heat better than tomato and runs through the cooler upper-Gulf summers, but in the hottest, most humid coastal areas it pauses through the peak before flushing again in fall. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. In the Imperial and Coachella Valleys, June through August daytime highs run past 105°F with nights above 80°F, and pepper flowers drop and pod set stops once days climb past about 90°F and nights hold above 75°F (Maryland extension notes evening temperatures above 75°F slow or stop pepper pod production). Even the heat-tolerant cayenne cannot set fruit through this, so desert growers run a late-winter crop that ripens before peak heat and a fall crop as the heat eases, leaving midsummer paused. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

The low-desert summer is a hard heat exclusion. In the Phoenix and Maricopa low desert, July and August daytime highs reach the 110s°F with nights above 80°F, and pepper flowers drop and pod set stops once days pass about 90°F and nights stay above 75°F. Even heat-tolerant cayenne cannot set fruit through this, so low-desert growers plant in February for a late-spring and early-summer crop and again as the heat eases for fall, leaving the deep-summer weeks paused. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

This is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. At the peak of summer the low desert (and the humid deep South) climbs past about 95°F by day and stays above 75°F at night, and pepper flowers drop and pod set stalls under those conditions (Maryland extension: pepper flowers and small fruits drop when nights stay above 75°F and days climb above 95°F, and plants often stop setting through midsummer). Habanero is a tropical Capsicum chinense that tolerates heat better than most peppers, so it runs straight through the milder warm-region summers, but even it pauses through the most extreme desert and deep-South heat before flushing again as the nights cool. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in deep-summer heat cucumber flowering and fruit set falter and the fruit turns bitter, which bites hardest on a small pickle whose skin carries most of the bitter compound. When daytime highs run in the 90s°F and higher with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and pollen so plants set poorly or drop young fruit, and heat-plus-drought stress drives the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) into what fruit does form. Set and quality recover as temperatures ease, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (regional extension planting chart; UMN Extension growing cucumbers)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap. Above about 90°F cucumber suffers reproductive failure: flowers and young fruit set poorly or drop, and set resumes once temperatures fall below the 90s. Heat builds fast under cover, so even protected plantings pause or lean on hard venting and shade through the hottest weeks, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (Penn State Extension, growing cucumbers in high tunnels; regional extension planting chart)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion for fava beans, not a frost gap. May through July is a summer gap on the south coast: lettuce bolts and germinates poorly as temperatures rise. The gap is softer than in the interior or desert (the maritime-influenced south coast stays milder) but still falls outside the Table 13.2 sowing window. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program)

April through August is excluded by extreme desert heat: soil and air well above the bolting threshold cause germination failure and bolting in lettuce. Imperial County summers run 90-120°F. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; UC Cooperative Extension, Imperial County)

value.zone_notes: Arizona low desert (USDA zone 9b; Maricopa County/Phoenix, Yuma). Frost is occasional and light; lettuce tolerates the rare light frost but not sustained heat. Last spring frost averages around February 15, but winter is mild growing weather for lettuce rather than a pause. The limiting factor is summer heat, not frost: triple-digit highs return in May and persist through August.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: May through August is excluded by extreme low-desert heat: soil and air well above the lettuce thermoinhibition range cause germination failure and bolting. In metro Phoenix the first 100°F day averages early May, and June through August average highs of about 104 to 106°F, far above the 77 to 95°F range that inhibits lettuce germination (University of Arizona AZ1099). April (average high about 85°F) is the spring bolting-close for an established crop rather than a no-sow month, and September is the soil-gated fall sow-resume, so the hard no-activity gap is May through August. (University of Arizona Cooperative Extension AZ1099; AZ1615)

value.zone_notes: Hawaii tropical (USDA zone 11; frost-free, frost_free_days 365). No frost anchor and no seasonal no-sow window for leaf lettuce. The limiting factor is summer heat quality, not a season boundary: in the hottest months leaf lettuce is grown with a heat-tolerant cultivar (Manoa, Anuenue) and afternoon shade, or moved to higher elevation, rather than paused. Heavy rain can bruise the soft leaves and is the other warm-month management concern.
value.calendar_basis: Leaf lettuce is grown YEAR-ROUND in tropical zone 11; both heat_pause and cold_pause are intentionally absent. There is no winter cold to pause for (frost-free) and no summer no-sow exclusion: University of Hawaii CTAHR lists green-leaf and red-leaf lettuce as year-round plantings at low elevation, and states leafy/semi-head types grow year-round at low elevations and in most home gardens. The summer heat brings a quality dip (tip-burn, faster bolting), managed with a heat-tolerant cultivar and afternoon shade or higher elevation, not a production stop. Absence of both pauses is intentional and carries this reason (standing principle: absence always carries a reason field); the year_round:true flag makes the all-active calendar's intent machine-readable. (University of Hawaii CTAHR RES-164; HGV-2)

The warm coastal zone 9 grows chard nearly year-round. UF and the Gulf calendars treat it as an excellent warm-weather green: it produces through the long warm season with even moisture and some shade, and the mild winter keeps it going, so one planting runs for months.

The hottest desert zone grows chard in the cool fall, winter, and spring, sown from September for a harvest October into May. The extreme peak summer, June through August, is excluded even for this heat-tolerant crop; the rest of the year is productive.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Swiss chard is one of the most heat-tolerant leafy greens and, unlike lettuce or spinach, it does not bolt in summer; across most regions it runs straight through the warm months. This cell is the exception: in the genuinely extreme summer of the extreme desert, sustained highs around and above 110°F push even chard past what it can hold, germination fails above about 85°F, and leaves scorch and stall, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop resumes in fall. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water, which chard tolerates better than spinach.

Summer gap is a heat-and-daylength exclusion, not a frost gap: bok choy is a cool-season Brassica rapa that bolts (sends up a seed stalk) and turns bitter once warm weather and long days arrive, and it will not form a tender upright rosette in summer heat. The planting calendar therefore splits into a short spring crop maturing before the heat and the main fall crop maturing as it breaks. (UMN Extension; Clemson HGIC)

Summer heat gap (Jul, Aug, Sep). Potato is a cool-season crop: tubers set and bulk best in cool soil, roughly 60 to 70°F, and tuber formation falls off sharply as the soil warms through summer, so the tops may keep growing while few usable tubers form. In the Southeast and Gulf the hot months sit outside the plant and harvest windows, which is why the extension planting calendars place potatoes in the cool season and skip the heat. (cool-season basis per Clemson; the 60 to 70°F optimum and ~80°F ceiling are modeled, not from a single T1 figure)

value.zone_notes: Along the warm Gulf coast (zone 9), cauliflower is a fall-planted winter crop: set transplants September-October for a harvest from December through early spring. The spring planting cabbage tolerates is dropped here, since cauliflower's curd will not size up before the Gulf heat arrives. LSU lists cole-crop transplants in fall. Summer is the off-season. Harvest months derived.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: cauliflower is a cool-season brassica that forms a firm white curd only in steady cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 75°F to 80°F (and hot nights above about 70°F) stops the plant from forming a proper curd and instead causes buttoning (tiny premature curds), ricing (a loose, grainy curd), and yellow-brown discoloration, so the crop is grown to mature in cool spring and fall and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. Along the warm Gulf coast cauliflower is grown only as a fall and winter crop; late spring through summer (May through August) is far too hot to curd, so those months are left out of the calendar. (LSU AgCenter, Clemson Cooperative Extension)

value.zone_notes: On the warm Southern California coast, cauliflower is a cool-season crop grown fall through spring. Set transplants in January-February for a spring harvest and again in September-October for a late-fall and winter harvest. The hottest weeks of summer can ruin curds, so the crop avoids midsummer. UC planting guides time cole crops for the cooler months here. Harvest months derived.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: cabbage is a cool-season brassica that forms firm, solid heads only in cool weather, roughly 60°F to 65°F. Sustained heat above about 80°F gives loose, open heads, triggers bolting, and worsens Fusarium yellows and cabbage aphid pressure, so the crop is grown to mature in cool spring and fall and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. Along the Gulf and lower coastal plain the long, hot, humid summer (June through August) excludes heading, so cabbage is a fall-through-spring crop and the hottest months are left out of the calendar. (LSU AgCenter, Clemson Cooperative Extension)

value.day_length_note_seasoned: At this latitude (below about 35 degrees N) grow short-day onions, which begin bulbing at just 10 to 12 hours of daylight. They are planted in fall or winter and bulb as days lengthen toward spring. A long-day variety here never reaches its longer daylength trigger and stays a leafy scallion that never forms a bulb.
value.day_length_note_beginner: Where you live, plant short-day onions. Day length means how many hours of sunlight there are in a day, and short-day onions make a bulb once days reach only 10 to 12 hours, which happens in your mild fall and winter. A northern (long-day) onion planted here would never make a bulb at all, just leaves.

value.zone_notes: Mildest south-coast zone 10: same fall-winter bulbing window; harvest late spring to summer. Intermediate-day, short-day also viable.
value.day_length_note_seasoned: The south-coastal latitude (roughly 33 to 34°N N) sits at the intermediate-to-short-day boundary. Intermediate-day onions (12 to 14 hours) are the dependable choice and bulb reliably here; short-day types (10 to 12 hours) also bulb at this lower latitude, so both are viable. Avoid long-day types, which may never reach their trigger.
value.day_length_note_beginner: Along the south coast you can grow either intermediate-day or short-day onions, since you are right on the line between them. Day length is how many daylight hours a day brings: intermediate-day onions bulb at about 12 to 14 hours and short-day ones at 10 to 12 hours, and both work here. Just avoid northern long-day onions, which may never form a bulb.

Deep summer in the low desert runs far too hot for sweet corn to pollinate: sustained highs well over 95°F kill pollen and desiccate the silks, so no reliable ears set from a midsummer planting. The crop is grown in the cooler months instead.

Midsummer highs in the low desert climb well past 95°F, which destroys corn pollen and dries out the silks, so ears set poorly. Sowings are timed to silk before or after this window rather than through it.

value.zone_notes: The hottest desert zone has the longest heat exclusion: sow from February through April for a May harvest before the extreme heat, skip the long furnace of June through August, and sow again in September for a late-fall and early-winter crop.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion here, not a frost gap. Edamame is a warm-season soybean that takes ordinary summer heat in stride, but through this region's extreme midsummer, sustained daytime temperatures above roughly 95 to 100°F cause soybean flowers and young pods to abort, so a crop set in the peak heat fails to fill. A spring sowing is harvested before the worst heat and a fall sowing goes in as it eases, leaving the hottest weeks out of the planting calendar.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Parsley is more heat-tolerant than most salad greens and does not bolt from heat, but in this region's extreme summer the foliage scorches and growth stalls, so the planting calendar pauses for these months and sowing resumes as the weather cools; plants already in the ground hang on with afternoon shade and steady water. The pause months here are modeled from the region's summer heat pattern.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Marginal in Hawaii, and viable mainly in cool, dry upcountry microclimates rather than the humid lowlands where most gardening happens. Where it succeeds, at higher, drier elevations with cool nights, thyme behaves as a low fragrant perennial; give it full sun, very sharp drainage, and lean, infrequent water. In the warm, humid lowlands it rots and is not a sound choice.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Thyme does not grow well in most of Hawaii because the lowlands are too hot and humid, which rots it. In cool, dry, higher-elevation spots with cool nights it can grow as a low fragrant perennial in a sunny, fast-draining spot. In the humid lowlands, it is best to skip it.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Eggplant is far more heat-tolerant than tomato or pepper and is one of the few fruiting crops that keeps setting through a hot summer, so it runs straight through the heat in nearly every region. The exception is the absolute extreme of the California desert valleys: in July and August, daytime highs reach well into the 110s°F with nights above 80°F, hot enough that even eggplant's pollen loses viability and fruit set stalls. Desert growers therefore run a spring crop that matures before peak heat and a fall crop set out in September as the heat eases, leaving midsummer paused. This pause reflects reduced fruit set at extreme heat, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

Eggplant is far more heat-tolerant than tomato or pepper and runs through summer heat in most regions, but Arizona's low desert is the extreme exception. In July and August, daytime highs reach the 110s°F with nights above 80°F, hot enough that even eggplant's pollen loses viability and fruit set stalls. Low-desert growers run a spring crop set out in February for an early-summer harvest and a fall crop set out as the heat eases, leaving the deep-summer weeks paused. This pause reflects reduced fruit set at extreme heat, not frost or cold. The exact pause months are modeled from the regional warm-season pattern.

The desert summer is a hard heat exclusion, not a frost gap. From June through August the low desert runs daytime highs well past 105°F with warm nights, and although tomatillo sets fruit better in heat than its tomato cousin, flower and pollen viability still fail once temperatures hold above about 95°F, so plants bloom without setting. Growers run a spring crop and a fall crop on either side of this window. (UC ANR Master Gardener; UC Statewide IPM)

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the warmer Gulf Coast zone 9, strawberries are grown on the same fall-planted annual system: set transplants from early October through mid November, with production starting as early as late November from plugs and running through spring into early summer, then remove the planting before the humid summer and replant the next fall. Raised rows with plastic or pine-straw mulch handle the heavy rain and keep fruit clean.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the warmer Gulf Coast areas, strawberries are still a winter crop you grow and then replace. Plant in October or early November, start picking as early as late fall, keep going through spring, then pull the plants before the humid summer and replant next fall. Use raised rows with plastic or pine straw for drainage.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 on the Gulf Coast sees occasional freezes; the plants are hardy to about 17°F but the open flowers are damaged below 32°F. Cover the bed with row-cover cloth when a freeze is forecast during bloom and anchor the edges.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: The warmest, frost-free south-coast pockets (zone 10) grow strawberries on the same fall-planted annual system: set transplants from mid August into late fall, with fall-set plants fruiting from winter into summer and the heaviest production in the first full season before the bed is replaced. With essentially no frost, day-neutral types can fruit across much of the year.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the mildest, frost-free parts of the south coast, plant strawberries in late summer or fall and replace them rather than keeping them for years. Fall-planted beds fruit from winter into summer, and with no frost some types keep producing much of the year.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is essentially frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is rarely a concern; the mild maritime climate, not cold, shapes the season.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the warmest low-desert pockets (zone 10), strawberries are still grown as a cool-season annual on the same fall-to-spring schedule: set pre-chilled plants in fall, fruit through winter and spring, then pull before summer. Zone 10 is nearly frost-free, so the season is bounded by heat rather than cold. Afternoon shade and well-drained, low-salt beds are essential.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the hottest, nearly frost-free parts of the California low desert, strawberries are a winter crop. Plant in fall, pick from late winter into spring, then pull the plants before the summer heat returns and replant next fall. Give them afternoon shade and good drainage.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the low desert is nearly frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is rarely a concern; the season is limited by summer heat, not cold. On a rare radiational freeze, cover open blossoms with frost cloth as a precaution.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Arizona's low desert (below 3,000 feet) grows strawberries as a cool-season annual rather than a perennial bed. Set dormant, pre-chilled (frigo) plants in fall, from mid September to mid November, fruit them through winter and spring, then pull and discard the planting before summer; the intense desert heat is too stressful to carry a bed over. Establish the bed where it gets morning sun but afternoon shade (a wall, fence, or 65 percent shade cloth) to reduce heat and water stress, and grow on well-drained beds because strawberries are sensitive to salty soil and water.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, strawberries are a cool-season crop you grow over the winter, not a bed that lives for years. Plant in fall, pick from late winter into spring, then pull the plants out before the hot summer and start fresh next fall. Give them morning sun but shade in the hot afternoon, and grow them where water drains away well.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The low desert sees a handful of freezing nights in December and January. Open blossoms and ripening fruit are damaged below 32°F, so on a night a freeze is forecast during bloom, cover the bed with frost cloth in the afternoon beforehand and anchor the edges. Frost pockets where cold air settles are best avoided.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In Hawaii (zone 11), strawberries are a cool-elevation niche crop, not a warm-lowland year-round one. They are grown upcountry, on the cool slopes of Haleakala (around Kula) and at Waimea on Hawaii Island, where conditions stay mild. At a fixed upcountry site, treat the bed as a short-lived perennial: set plants in the cool fall months for a main crop through winter and spring. Year-round supply exists in Hawaii only because commercial farms move harvest up and down the mountain with the seasons, which a single home garden cannot replicate. In the warm lowlands strawberries perform poorly.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In Hawaii, strawberries grow best up in the cool higher country, like Kula on Maui, not down in the warm lowlands. Plant in the cool fall months and you will get berries through winter and spring. The big farms have berries all year because they move up and down the mountain with the seasons, but in a home garden at one spot you will get a cool-season crop, not year-round fruit.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Upcountry Hawaii (zone 11) is frost-free, so freeze injury to blossoms is not a concern. The practical season is set by the mild upcountry temperatures and elevation rather than by cold; warm spells, not frost, end the crop at a given site.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Southeast is a chill-limited edge: low-chill Japanese plums (Methley, Santa Rosa) crop, but European types rarely bank enough chill. Expect a lighter, less certain crop and high disease pressure.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Southeast is a warm edge where low-chill Japanese plums like Methley and Santa Rosa fruit, but European plums usually cannot get enough winter cold. Expect a lighter crop and watch for disease.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Warm winters, not frost, are the main limit here; a mild winter can leave even low-chill types blooming unevenly.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the South Coast banks too little winter chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours) for even low-chill plums to fruit dependably; a tree may survive and bloom sparsely but should not be counted on for a crop.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the South Coast is too mild in winter for plums to fruit dependably. A tree may live and bloom a little, but do not count on plums.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the California desert banks too little winter chill (about 100 to 300 hours) for plums to fruit reliably, and extreme summer heat compounds it; a tree may survive but should not be relied on for a crop.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the California desert is too mild in winter and too hot in summer for plums to fruit reliably. A tree may survive but will rarely give plums.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Arizona's low desert banks little chill (about 100 to 400 hours), so only the lowest-chill Japanese plums (Methley) crop, and only in cooler winters; blistering summer heat and heavy irrigation demand make it a challenging, marginal plum site.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Arizona's low desert gets very little winter chill, so only the lowest-chill Japanese plums like Methley fruit, and only in cooler winters. The extreme summer heat makes it a tough, marginal spot for plums.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Low winter chill and extreme summer heat, not frost, are the limits; the tree needs heavy irrigation.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Tropical zone 11 in Hawaii banks essentially no winter chill (0 to 150 hours); European and Japanese plums cannot break dormancy and will not fruit. Not a plum zone.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Tropical Hawaii has almost no winter cold, so European and Japanese plums cannot bloom or fruit here. This is not a plum-growing zone.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 Gulf is marginal and difficult: chill suits only low-chill cultivars, erratic warm winters push very early bloom into frost, and humid heat drives severe disease. Only a low-chill, disease-tolerant cultivar on a frost-safe, well-drained site is worth attempting.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the Gulf is a hard place for apricots: only low-chill kinds get enough cold, the tree blooms very early into frost, and the humid heat brings heavy disease. Only a low-chill, disease-tough variety on a well-drained, frost-safe spot is worth a try.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Very early bloom driven by warm winters is frequently frosted, and humid heat compounds the loss with disease; a dependable crop is unlikely.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 South Coast usually cannot bank enough winter chill for even low-chill apricots, so the tree survives and grows but blooms erratically and rarely sets a dependable crop. Treat it as a tree that lives rather than one that fruits.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the South Coast is usually too mild to give even low-chill apricots the cold they need, so the tree lives and grows but blooms unevenly and rarely fruits dependably. Treat it as a tree that survives rather than one that crops.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 California desert usually cannot deliver enough chill for even low-chill apricots, so the tree survives without a dependable crop. Chill shortage, not frost, is the limiting factor at this warm desert edge.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the California desert usually does not get cold enough even for low-chill apricots, so the tree survives but does not reliably fruit. Here it is a shortage of winter cold, not frost, that is the problem.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 Arizona low desert is marginal and strictly low-chill: only cultivars needing about 400 hours or less will bloom, and even those crop only after colder winters. Bloom and harvest are very early, the dry air keeps disease low, and hard frosts are uncommon, so chill is the limiting factor.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert is marginal and strictly for low-chill kinds: only varieties needing about 400 hours or less will bloom, and even those fruit mainly after colder winters. Bloom and harvest come very early, the dry air keeps disease down, and hard frosts are rare, so winter cold is the limit.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard late frosts are uncommon in the low desert; the crop is limited by marginal chill rather than frost, so a colder winter yields a crop and a mild one may not.

Zone lows of 20 to 30°F reach the high-20s°F range where lime foliage and fruit are damaged, so a crop is dependable only in milder years and with active freeze protection. Key lime will not crop here; Persian lime is the only real option and only with protection.

Zone lows of 28 to 38°F reach the high-20s°F range where lime foliage and fruit are damaged, so a crop is dependable only in milder years and with active freeze protection. Ideal heat, but Arizona's periodic hard freezes take tender limes first.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Limes can fruit here, but cold winters can wipe out a crop. You will get fruit in milder years if you cover the tree when a freeze is coming. Protect the tree whenever a hard freeze is forecast.
value.harvest: Jun - Nov (desert heat; first citrus lost in a hard freeze)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is the main risk to the crop. Zone lows of 28 to 38°F reach or pass the high-20s°F point where lime fruit and leaves are damaged; cover the tree or move a container under cover on freeze nights, and pick ripe fruit ahead of a hard freeze.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Frost-free tropical lowland Hawaii fruits limes continuously year-round, with the everbearing habit fully expressed. Cold is a non-issue; disease and pest pressure are the focus.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Limes fruit year-round in tropical Hawaii with no frost worry at all. Just manage pests and diseases.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is not a factor here. Lows do not approach the high-20s°F damage point, so no cold protection is needed.

value.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely hold below the mid-20s°F long enough to take the crop, and summer heat is more than enough to sweeten a navel. Cold protection is an occasional need, not a routine one.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Oranges do well in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that you usually keep your fruit, and summers are plenty hot to make it sweet.
value.harvest: Nov - Jan (and holding on the tree into late winter)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf region is mostly safe for navels, but hard freezes do occur in some winters. Temperatures dropping below 27°F can damage ripe fruit and scorch young growth, while most winters stay mild enough that no intervention is needed. Have frost cloth or a heat source ready for the tree's first few winters while it is still small and the canopy is less thermally buffered.

value.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is frost-safe but heat-marginal: a navel ripens but is more tart and less deeply colored than inland fruit. Reduced quality, not failure, and not a cold issue; the immediate fog-belt runs cooler still and pushes quality lower.
value.suitability_note_beginner: In zone 10 on the south coast the tree thrives and never freezes, but mild summers leave the fruit only middling, less sweet than inland oranges. Right on the foggy coast it is even cooler and the fruit is more sour.
value.harvest: Jan - Apr (holds long on the tree; sweetness builds slowly in the mild coast climate)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; the limiting factor is borderline summer heat, not winter cold.

value.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); avoid planting into peak summer heat
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the low desert fruits reliably and at high quality: abundant summer heat sweetens and colors the navel fully, and winter frost only rarely threatens the crop. Manage spring fruit-drop with adequate irrigation.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the desert is excellent for oranges. Lots of summer heat makes them sweet and deeply colored, and frost is rarely a problem. Just water well in spring.
value.harvest: Dec - Mar (early selections can start late October; Washington Dec into March)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s°F reach colder desert sites; mature trees tolerate this, but young trees benefit from protection on the coldest nights.

value.plant_out: Spring (container or balled); avoid planting into peak summer heat
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert fruits reliably and at high quality: abundant summer heat fully sweetens and colors the navel, and frost rarely threatens the crop. Spring irrigation manages the heat-driven fruit-drop.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona desert is excellent for oranges. Hot summers make them sweet and deeply colored, and frost is rarely a problem. Just water well in spring.
value.harvest: Dec - Mar (Washington navel; early selections can start late October)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Only occasional light frost reaches the Arizona low desert; mature navels tolerate it, and crop loss to cold is rare.

value.plant_out: Year-round (container or balled) in this frost-free climate
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 in Hawaii is frost-free and grows navels year-round, but quality is marginal: the warm, humid tropics lack the cool nights needed to sweeten and color the fruit, so low-elevation navels stay tart and green-skinned. Cooler uplands improve quality. Not a cold or heat-shortage issue, a diurnal-swing one.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 11 in Hawaii grows oranges all year and never freezes, but the fruit is often sour and stays green because the nights do not get cool enough to sweeten it. It is better up in the cooler hills.
value.harvest: Oct - Jan (Washington navel; lower-elevation fruit stays green-tinged and tart)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: There is no frost risk in Hawaii; the limiting factor is the lack of cool nights for quality, not cold.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably and easily: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely threaten a hardy mandarin, and the heat is ample for good quality. Satsuma, clementine, and late types all do well; cold protection is an occasional need, not routine.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Mandarins do great in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that the tree and crop are safe, and summers are plenty warm for good fruit.
value.harvest: Nov - Jan (satsuma into clementine; a few late types hold longer)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf is mostly safe for mandarins; hard freezes occur in some winters, so keep frost cloth ready for young trees.

value.plant_out: Most of the year (spring ideal) in this frost-free climate
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is prime mandarin territory: frost-free, with enough warmth for good quality. This is the home of the famous Ojai Pixie and of excellent clementine and Gold Nugget crops. Mandarins do markedly better here than a navel, which is only middling on this coast.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the south coast is excellent for mandarins. It never freezes and is warm enough for sweet fruit; this is where the famous Ojai Pixie mandarins grow. Mandarins beat oranges here.
value.harvest: Dec - Mar (early satsuma through late Pixie and Gold Nugget)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a crop factor on the south coast; a hardy mandarin is well within its cold range here.

value.plant_out: Spring; avoid planting into peak summer heat
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the low desert fruits reliably: abundant summer heat and rare winter frost. Clementine and late mandarins such as W. Murcott thrive on the heat; satsuma prefers the milder end and can run softer in flavor in extreme heat. Manage spring fruit-drop with steady irrigation.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the desert is good for mandarins, with lots of summer heat and little frost. Clementines and late types love the heat; satsuma does better where it is a bit milder. Water well in spring so the tree keeps its fruit.
value.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late mandarins; satsuma earlier)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Occasional radiation frosts into the upper 20s°F reach colder desert sites; mature mandarins tolerate this, and young trees benefit from protection on the coldest nights.

value.plant_out: Spring; avoid planting into peak summer heat
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert fruits reliably: abundant summer heat and rare frost. Clementine and late mandarins ripen richly; satsuma runs earlier and prefers the milder end. Spring irrigation manages the heat-driven fruit-drop.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona desert grows good mandarins, with hot summers and little frost. Clementines love the heat, and satsuma ripens earliest. Water well in spring so the tree holds its fruit.
value.harvest: Nov - Feb (clementine and late types; satsuma earlier)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Only occasional light frost reaches the Arizona low desert; mature mandarins tolerate it and crop loss to cold is rare.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent, nearly frost-free fig country with a long ripening season. Figs crop heavily; the main management is humid-weather rust and souring and, in sandy soil, root-knot nematodes. Favor closed-eye, rust-tolerant varieties.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent, almost frost-free fig country with a long season. Figs bear heavily here; the main jobs are managing rust and souring in humid weather and nematodes in sandy soil. Grow a tight-eye, rust-tolerant variety.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Warm, frost-free, and sunny: excellent for figs, with a long season that ripens full, sweet crops and low disease pressure. Almost any common variety thrives; keep water steady and net against birds.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Warm, frost-free, and sunny: excellent for figs, with a long season that ripens big, sweet crops and little disease. Almost any common variety does well; keep water steady and net against birds.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent, nearly frost-free desert fig country. This is exactly where a fig's low chill need pays off: heavy, high-quality crops in heat that defeats high-chill trees. Keep deep summer water going and net against birds.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent, almost frost-free desert fig country. This is just where figs' low need for cold pays off: big, high-quality crops in heat that beats high-chill trees. Keep the deep summer water going and net against birds.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Excellent low-desert fig country: intense heat and a long season ripen heavy crops, and the mild winter easily meets the small chill need. Deep, frequent summer water is essential; both crops ripen well and disease is low.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Excellent low-desert fig country: intense heat and a long season ripen big crops, and the mild winter easily gives figs the little cold they need. Deep, frequent summer water is a must; both crops ripen well and disease is low.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Marginal for dependable cropping. Figs grow and set fruit, but near-absent dormancy plus high humidity, fig rust, souring, and nematodes make yields erratic and quality variable. Grow in a container of clean mix, choose a rust-tolerant small-eye variety, and keep up sanitation.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Marginal for a dependable crop. Figs grow and set fruit, but with almost no winter rest and lots of humidity, rust, souring, and nematodes, the crop is up and down. Grow it in a pot of clean mix, pick a rust-tolerant tight-eye variety, and keep the plant and ground clean.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 Gulf has abundant heat and a long season but the region's humidity and rainfall still cap fruit quality through disease and splitting. Marginal: reliable growth, unreliable clean fruit. Choose open, airy, well-drained ground.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 on the Gulf has lots of heat and a long season, but the humidity and rain still limit fruit quality through disease and splitting. Marginal: the plant grows well, the fruit is iffy. Choose an open, airy, well-drained spot.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 South Coast is frost-free and warm but the immediate coast's cooler, moister summers make it marginal for peak quality. It fruits well on the warmest, sunniest sites; quality is best inland from the fog.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the South Coast is frost-free and warm, but the cooler, damper air right at the coast makes it only okay for top-quality fruit. It fruits well in the warmest, sunniest spots; the best fruit is inland from the fog.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 desert is the hottest, earliest-ripening pomegranate ground: superb color and sweetness, minimal disease, low chill easily met. Prioritize even, deep irrigation to prevent split in the extreme heat.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 in the desert is the hottest, earliest-ripening spot: superb color and sweetness, little disease, and plenty of the low winter cold it needs. Focus on even, deep watering to prevent splitting in the extreme heat.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 Arizona low desert is prime: intense heat and dry air ripen deeply colored, sweet fruit early with minimal disease, and chill is met. Even, deep irrigation to prevent split is the main discipline.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert is prime: intense heat and dry air ripen deep-colored, sweet fruit early with little disease, and there is enough winter cold. Even, deep watering to prevent splitting is the main task.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 11 Hawaii is frost-free but banks essentially no winter chill and is humid, so pomegranate does not go dormant properly and does not fruit reliably. The plant survives and may flower but should be treated as an ornamental.

value.type_note_seasoned: Standard raspberries fail in the hot, humid Southeast; the one type worth growing is a heat-tolerant, low-chill trailing raspberry such as Dorman Red, which fruits in early summer and tolerates the heat and disease pressure that defeat northern reds. It is trained on a trellis like a trailing blackberry.
value.type_note_beginner: Most raspberries cannot take the hot, humid Southeast. The one that works is a heat-tolerant, low-chill type like Dorman Red, which fruits in early summer and is grown on a trellis like a trailing blackberry.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Trailing low-chill raspberries bloom in late winter to early spring, so a late freeze can catch open bloom; choose a protected site and be ready to cover plants on cold nights.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Gulf South a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, heat-tolerant trailing cane fruit, planted while dormant in winter; it blooms in early spring and ripens an early-summer crop before the worst heat, then is pruned and retrained in the dormant season. Only the low-chill, heat-tolerant types persist here, and even those are best treated as a short-lived novelty.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Deep South, raspberries are grown as a heat-tolerant trailing type, planted in winter while dormant. They flower in early spring and ripen in early summer before the worst heat. Only special low-chill types will keep going here, and even those may not last many years.

value.type_note_seasoned: The mild southern coast has limited winter chill, so grow low-chill everbearing reds and give afternoon shade a short distance inland. Coastal cool keeps plants comfortable; the further from the ocean, the more heat and shade management matter.
value.type_note_beginner: The mild southern coast does not get very cold, so grow low-chill everbearing red raspberries. Right on the coast they take full sun; a little inland, give them afternoon shade.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is seldom a problem on the southern coast; low-chill types bloom early, so an inland late frost can occasionally nip bloom, but summer heat and dry air are the bigger stresses.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: On the mild southern coast a raspberry is grown as a deciduous, low-chill cane fruit; the gentle winter banks just enough chill for budbreak, and it blooms in late winter and ripens in late spring before summer heat. Plant dormant in winter, give afternoon shade away from the immediate coast, and keep it well-watered.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: On the mild southern coast, raspberries rest through a gentle winter, flower in late winter, and ripen in late spring before it gets hot. Plant in winter, give afternoon shade if you are inland, and water well.

value.type_note_seasoned: California's low desert is at the hot, low-chill extreme for raspberries: only the most heat-tolerant, low-chill everbearing types have any chance, and only with afternoon-to-full shade, heavy mulch, and abundant water. Treat it as a difficult experiment, not a dependable crop.
value.type_note_beginner: The California low desert is about the hardest place to grow raspberries. Only the toughest heat-tolerant types might work, and only with lots of shade, mulch, and water. Treat it as an experiment.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue in the low desert; intense heat, sun, and dry air are what defeat raspberries here, so shade and water are everything.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the low desert a raspberry can only be attempted as a deciduous, low-chill cane fruit nursed through extreme heat: planted dormant in winter, it blooms in late winter and must finish a small crop in spring before the brutal summer, under heavy shade and constant water. Most plantings are short-lived.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the low desert, raspberries can only be attempted with heavy shade and constant water. Plant in winter, hope for a small spring crop before the extreme summer heat, and expect the plants not to last long.

value.type_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert is among the least suitable climates for raspberries: extreme heat and almost no winter chill defeat standard reds entirely. Only the most heat-tolerant, low-chill everbearing types are worth a trial, under full shade with heavy mulch and constant water.
value.type_note_beginner: The Arizona low desert is one of the worst climates for raspberries. The heat and lack of winter cold defeat normal types. Only the toughest heat-tolerant kinds are worth trying, with full shade and constant water.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely the issue in the low desert; relentless heat, intense sun, and dry air are what kill raspberries here, so shade and water are the whole game.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In the Arizona low desert a raspberry can only be attempted as a deciduous, low-chill cane fruit nursed through extreme conditions: planted dormant in winter, it must finish a small crop in spring before the searing summer, under full shade, deep mulch, and constant irrigation. Plantings are typically short-lived.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, raspberries can only be attempted with full shade, deep mulch, and constant water. Plant in winter and hope for a small spring crop before the extreme summer. The plants usually do not last long.

value.type_note_seasoned: Raspberries are essentially unsuited to lowland tropical Hawaii, which provides no winter chill. They can only be attempted at cool high elevations, where a low-chill, heat-tolerant everbearing type might ripen a small crop. Wild thimbleberry-type Rubus grow in the islands, but cultivated raspberry is a marginal novelty here.
value.type_note_beginner: Raspberries do not grow in lowland tropical Hawaii, which never gets cold enough. They might be tried only in cool high-elevation spots, and even then a crop is uncertain. Other fruits are a much better fit for the islands.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The tropical lowlands are frost-free and far too warm for raspberries; only cool high-elevation microclimates offer enough relief, and even there the lack of real winter chill limits cropping.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In Hawaii a cultivated raspberry can only be attempted at cool high elevation, as a low-chill, heat-tolerant cane fruit that never gets a true winter; with minimal dormancy it may push a small, uncertain crop in spring. In the warm lowlands it simply will not fruit, and it is best regarded as an experiment.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In Hawaii, raspberries can only be tried at cool high elevations, and even then a crop is uncertain because there is no real winter. In the warm lowlands they will not fruit. Treat it as an experiment, not a reliable crop.

value.type_note_seasoned: Zone 9 grows low-chill erect thornless blackberries well, with the crop ripening from May into June ahead of peak summer heat. Choose the lowest-chill, most heat- and rosette-tolerant cultivars (Natchez, Kiowa, Ouachita).
value.type_note_beginner: Zone 9 grows low-chill upright thornless blackberries well, ripening in May and June before the worst heat. Pick the lowest-chill, most heat-tolerant kinds.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Low-chill blackberries bloom in late winter to early spring, so a late freeze can catch open bloom; choose a protected site and be ready to cover plants on cold nights.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Here a blackberry is grown as a deciduous cane fruit: the canes drop their leaves and rest through winter, banking the chill the plant needs, while the perennial crown and roots live for 15 to 20 years and each cane lives only two, growing one year and fruiting the next before dying. You prune in the dormant season, matching the cut to habit and type. Planted once, a patch fruits for two decades.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Your blackberry loses its leaves and rests through winter (this rest is called dormancy). The roots live for years, but each cane lives only two: it grows one year, then fruits and dies. You prune in winter, and how you prune depends on the type. Plant once and a patch keeps producing for many years.

value.type_note_seasoned: Blackberries are essentially unsuited to lowland tropical Hawaii, which provides no winter chill. They can only be attempted at cool high elevations, where a low-chill primocane-fruiting type might ripen a small, uncertain crop. Cultivated blackberry is a marginal novelty here.
value.type_note_beginner: Blackberries do not grow in lowland tropical Hawaii, which never gets cold enough. They might be tried only in cool high-elevation spots, and even then a crop is uncertain. Other fruits are a much better fit for the islands.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The tropical lowlands are frost-free and far too warm for blackberries; only cool high-elevation microclimates offer enough relief, and even there the lack of real winter chill limits cropping.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: In Hawaii a cultivated blackberry can only be attempted at cool high elevation, as a low-chill cane fruit that never gets a true winter; with minimal dormancy it may push a small, uncertain crop in spring. In the warm lowlands it simply will not fruit.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: In Hawaii, blackberries can only be tried at cool high elevations, and even then a crop is uncertain because there is no real winter. In the warm lowlands they will not fruit. Treat it as an experiment.

value.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the type to grow; there is no separate warm-climate type as there is for blueberry. It grows and fruits here but wants steady moisture and appreciates some relief from extreme heat. Plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
value.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, the one common type. It will grow here with plenty of water, but it likes a real winter, so it is a bit less reliable in the warmest spots. Plant two different varieties for a good crop.
value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Elderberry is a permanent deciduous shrub here too, planted once and kept for years, though in the mild winters it rests only briefly. It blooms in spring and ripens earlier than in the North; keep it well watered through the heat, renew old canes in late winter, and plant two different cultivars for good fruit set.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Your elderberry is a long-lived bush you plant once and keep for years. In the mild winters here it rests only briefly, flowers in spring, and ripens earlier than up North. Keep it well watered in the heat, prune old stems in late winter, and plant two different varieties.

value.type_note_seasoned: American elderberry is the only type to try, and this is its warm, low-chill, high-heat edge: it grows and can fruit, but treat it as marginal, give it ample water and afternoon shade, and still plant two different cultivars for cross-pollination.
value.type_note_beginner: Grow American elderberry, but know this is a tough spot for it: hot summers and mild winters make it iffy. Give it lots of water and some afternoon shade, and plant two different varieties. Treat it as an experiment.
