value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm Gulf edge fruits Asian persimmon (Fuyu, Hachiya) reliably given persimmon's low chill need, with an early, long harvest. American persimmon also fruits well. Disease and drainage are the variables, not chill.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The warm Gulf edge fruits Asian persimmon like Fuyu and Hachiya reliably, since persimmon needs little cold, with a long harvest. American persimmon does well too. The things to watch are disease and drainage, not cold.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest coastal zone 10 banks low chill (about 50 to 350 hours), so low-chill Asian cultivars (Fuyu, Izu) fruit but marginally, lighter in warm winters. The tree grows easily; the crop is the variable.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The warmest coast gets little winter cold, so low-chill Asian kinds like Fuyu and Izu fruit but only marginally, lighter in warm winters. The tree grows easily; the crop is the uncertain part.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest desert zone 10 barely meets low-chill needs and pushes fruit into brutal summer heat and sunburn; only the lowest-chill, earliest cultivars are worth trying, and crops are light and uncertain.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert zone 10 barely gets enough winter cold and bakes the fruit in extreme summer heat and sunburn. Only the lowest-chill, earliest kinds are worth trying, and crops are light and uncertain.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-desert zone 9 banks roughly 100 to 400 chill hours, just meeting low-chill Asian cultivars (Izu near 100, Fuyu near 200), but intense summer heat and sunburn keep it marginal. UA notes Fuyu as nearly pest-free and suited to hot climates; plant low-chill, water generously, and protect fruit from the worst sun.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Low-desert zone 9 gets just enough winter cold for low-chill Asian kinds like Izu and Fuyu, but intense summer heat and sunburn keep it marginal. Arizona extension notes Fuyu as nearly pest-free and good for hot climates; plant a low-chill variety, water well, and shade the fruit from the worst sun.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Lowland tropical Hawaii banks essentially no chill (well under 150 hours), below even low-chill Asian persimmon's need, so standard cultivars grow as attractive trees but do not fruit reliably at low elevation. (Cooler upland Hawaii, outside this region, does grow persimmon.)
value.suitability_note_beginner: Lowland tropical Hawaii gets almost no winter cold, less than even low-chill Asian persimmon needs, so ordinary varieties grow as nice trees but do not fruit reliably down low. (Hawaii's cooler high country, not this region, does grow persimmon.)

value.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, lower-chill Gulf edge. Favor lower-chill and red mulberry types; these fruit early and heavily. Popcorn disease pressure is highest on white types in this humid warmth, so sanitation matters.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The warm, lower-chill edge near the Gulf. Choose lower-chill or red mulberry types, which fruit early and heavily. Popcorn disease is most likely on white types in this humid warmth, so keep things clean.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom is early here, but mulberry's later leaf-out and quick recovery keep frost from being a real threat.

value.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, low-chill edge. Lower-chill and black mulberries fruit here, but the mildest winters bank little chill, so favor genuinely low-chill cultivars (Pakistan, Black Beauty, dwarf types); higher-chill hybrids may bloom and fruit erratically.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The warm, low-chill edge. Lower-chill and black mulberries fruit here, but the mildest winters give little cold, so choose truly low-chill types like Pakistan, Black Beauty, or a dwarf; higher-chill hybrids can fruit unevenly.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is essentially a non-issue in this mild zone.

value.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert edge. Low-chill and black mulberries fruit early with irrigation, but the mildest winters bank little chill, so stick to genuinely low-chill cultivars and expect a very early, heat-driven harvest.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest, lowest-chill desert edge. Low-chill and black mulberries fruit early if watered, but winters give little cold, so stick to truly low-chill varieties and expect a very early, heat-driven harvest.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is essentially a non-issue in this warm zone.

value.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Fruits very early with irrigation and a low-chill cultivar. The extreme heat and low chill make this a low-chill-only zone; well-watered low-chill and black types crop well, but higher-chill hybrids fruit erratically.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Fruits very early with watering and a low-chill variety. The extreme heat and low chill make this a low-chill-only zone; well-watered low-chill and black types do well, but higher-chill hybrids fruit unevenly.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is a minor early concern; mulberry's late leaf-out keeps it largely clear.

value.plant_out: Late winter to early spring (dormant, bare-root)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-chill and white mulberries fruit in the tropical warmth, with a long or intermittent harvest rather than a single flush, since the tree barely goes dormant. Treat it as a warm-climate, low-chill planting; birds and the staining drop are the main management issues.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Low-chill and white mulberries fruit in the tropical warmth, over a long or on-and-off season rather than all at once, since the tree barely rests. Treat it as a warm-climate, low-chill planting; birds and the staining fruit drop are the main things to manage.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, humid Gulf edge of pawpaw's range: it grows and fruits here, but very mild winters can run short of the roughly 400 chill hours pawpaw needs, so bloom and set are less reliable in the warmest years. Choose southern-adapted selections.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The warm, humid Gulf edge of where pawpaw grows: it fruits here, but very mild winters can be short on the winter cold pawpaw needs, so flowering and fruit set are less reliable in the warmest years. Choose southern-adapted kinds.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: At the warm, low-chill southern edge (about 350 chill hours), very mild winters can leave the tree short of the cold it needs for even bloom and good set, so fruiting is less dependable.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The mildest south-coast zone has essentially no winter chill and a warm, dry climate; it is not a pawpaw site.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The mildest south-coast areas have almost no winter cold and a warm, dry climate; this is not a place for pawpaw.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: As in desert zone 9, only harsher: heat, aridity, and minimal chill make this unsuitable for pawpaw.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Like desert zone 9, only harsher: heat, dryness, and little winter cold make this no place for pawpaw.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The low desert's extreme heat and aridity are the opposite of the cool, humid, shaded conditions pawpaw needs; it is not viable here.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The low desert's extreme heat and dryness are the opposite of the cool, humid, shaded conditions pawpaw needs; it will not grow here.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Despite its tropical-tasting fruit, pawpaw is a temperate tree that needs a cold winter to break dormancy; tropical Hawaii provides no chill, so it is unsuitable.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Parsnip is a cool-season root that germinates and grows best at roughly 50 to 70°F and develops its sweet flavor only after near-freezing weather, so in the Southeast and Gulf the late-spring and summer months (Apr, May, Jun, Jul, Aug) are far too hot to sow or grow it. The crop is handled as a fall-sown, winter-harvested vegetable, and those hot months carry no sowing or active growth. (Clemson HGIC; Texas A&M AgriLife)

value.zone_notes: In the frost-free zone-10 pockets the roots still size up, but with little cold they sweeten less than parsnips grown where hard frosts occur.

The crop is handled as a fall-sown, winter-harvested vegetable, and those hot months carry no sowing or active growth. (UC ANR Master Gardener Program; Texas A&M AgriLife)

value.zone_notes: Parsnip is not recommended for tropical-lowland Hawaii: no cool season and no frost to sweeten the roots. Window is a flagged model for roster completeness only; cooler upland elevations would do better.

value.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 fruits reliably: mild Gulf and Southeastern winters rarely hold below the mid-20s°F long enough to take the crop, and long hot summers bank plenty of heat to sweeten grapefruit over its long hang. Cold protection is an occasional need, not a routine one.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit does well in zone 9. Winters are mild enough that you usually keep your fruit, and summers are plenty hot to make it sweet over its long season.
value.harvest: Nov - May (holds and sweetens on the tree into spring)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Zone 9 across the Gulf is mostly safe for grapefruit, but hard freezes occur in some winters; below about 27°F can damage ripe fruit and scorch young growth. Keep frost cloth ready for the tree's first few winters while it is small.

value.plant_out: Most of the year (container or balled; spring ideal)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 on the south coast is essentially frost-free but only marginally hot for grapefruit; fruit ripens slowly and often stays tart, so a low-acid hybrid is the better choice.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Zone 10 on the south coast almost never freezes, but it is only marginally hot enough for grapefruit, so the fruit ripens slowly and can stay tart.
value.harvest: Feb - Jun (ripens slowly in the mild coast; often stays tart)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: The immediate coast in zone 10 is nearly frost-free; heat, not cold, is the limiter.

value.plant_out: Fall or spring (container or balled; avoid mid-summer planting stress)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 10 in the low desert fruits reliably and superbly: sustained intense heat ripens deeply sweet red grapefruit over a long season, with fruit best late in the season. Cold is only an occasional concern.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit is excellent in desert zone 10. The heat makes it deeply sweet, best late in the season. Cold is rarely a problem.
value.harvest: Dec - May (best Mar to May; holds and sweetens on the tree)
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Hard frosts are infrequent in zone 10 desert but do occur; protect young trees on the coldest nights.

value.plant_out: Fall or spring (container or balled; avoid mid-summer planting stress)
value.suitability_note_seasoned: Zone 9 in the Arizona low desert fruits reliably and superbly: intense sustained heat over a long season ripens deeply sweet, low-acid red grapefruit. The coldest winter nights near freezing are the only real risk, mainly to young trees and fruit.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Grapefruit is excellent in Arizona desert zone 9. The intense heat makes it deeply sweet over a long season. Just protect young trees and fruit on the coldest nights.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmer, lower-chill zone 9 Gulf edge combines marginal chill with intense heat, humidity, and harvest-season rain, all of which sweet cherry handles badly. Disease pressure and cracking make it an unsuitable crop here regardless of cultivar.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The warmer Gulf edge is too mild in winter and too hot, humid, and rainy in season for sweet cherry. It is not a workable crop here.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 150 chill hours, well below even the lowest-chill sweet cherry. The tree grows in the mild climate but the blossoms drop without setting fruit. This is a no-crop case, not a marginal one.
value.suitability_note_beginner: In the warmest coastal areas, winters are far too mild for sweet cherry to fruit, even the low-chill kinds. The tree will grow but give essentially no fruit.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert sites bank under about 150 chill hours, far below any sweet cherry, and the fierce summer heat compounds the problem. The tree survives the heat poorly and does not fruit. Not a sweet cherry location.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert spots are far too mild in winter and too hot in summer for sweet cherry. Expect little to no fruit, and a tree that struggles in the heat.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert banks only about 100 to 400 chill hours, below even the low-chill sweet cherry's roughly 250-hour need in most winters, and the extreme summer heat is hostile to the crop. Sweet cherry is unsuitable here; the low desert grows low-chill peaches, apricots, and figs instead.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The Arizona low desert is too mild in winter and far too hot in summer for sweet cherry. It will not get the cold it needs and cannot take the heat, so it is not a workable crop. Grow low-chill peaches, apricots, or figs instead.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Hawaii banks effectively zero chill, far below the requirement of any sweet cherry cultivar. Sweet cherry will not fruit; this is a genuine no-grow case, not a marginal one. Tropical and subtropical fruits are the adapted choices.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Sweet cherry needs cold winters to fruit, and Hawaii does not have them. It will not grow fruit here. Grow tropical fruits instead.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer heat exclusion (May, Jun, Jul, Aug). Turnip is a cool-season crop that grows and tastes best around 60 to 65°F; sustained summer heat above about 75°F turns the roots woody, pithy, and sharp-flavored, slows germination, and pushes plants to bolt, so turnips are grown as a fall-through-spring crop here and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; LSU AgCenter)

Hot desert valley: fall-planted leeks harvested late winter into spring. The intense summer is skipped entirely.
Low desert Arizona: a cool-season winter crop. Start seed in early fall, transplant late fall into early winter, and harvest late winter into spring before the extreme heat returns.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: brussels sprouts are a cool-season brassica that builds a leafy stalk in mild weather but sets firm, tight sprouts only when temperatures cool, roughly into the 60°F to 65°F range. Through the hot months the plant either stalls or makes loose, leafy, bitter sprouts, and cabbage aphid pressure peaks, so the crop is grown to mature in the cool season and the hottest months are left out of the planting calendar. Along the Gulf and lower coastal plain the long, hot, humid summer makes poor, aphid-prone sprouts, so brussels sprouts are strictly a fall-through-spring crop. (Clemson Cooperative Extension; LSU AgCenter)

value.zone_notes: In the mildest south-coast zone brussels sprouts crop through winter and well into spring from a fall set; only the hottest midsummer weeks are excluded.

value.zone_notes: A short cool-season window only: transplant in early fall and harvest in winter; spring and summer are the off-season. Harvest months are derived from the planting window and maturity.

In the Arizona low desert brussels sprouts are a winter crop: the University of Arizona Maricopa calendar lists sowing from about August to mid-October, with transplants set in early fall, for a harvest through the cool winter into early spring. Summer is the long off-season.

Brussels sprouts are marginal in lowland tropical Hawaii: a cool-season window only, with firmer sprouts at cooler elevations. The window is modeled on CTAHR cole-crop guidance because the cited bulletin (B-91) is a 1943 scanned PDF that did not parse and does not table brussels months directly.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warm, lower-chill Gulf edge. Winters bank only about 500 to 650 chill hours, so favor lower-chill cultivars (around 500 to 600 hours); the high-chill set will not fruit reliably. Very early bloom raises frost exposure in cool springs.
value.suitability_note_beginner: This warmer edge can grow nectarines, but only lower-chill varieties, and some winters are too mild for a full crop. Choose a low-chill variety.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Bloom comes very early here, so even a mild late freeze can catch open flowers. Lower-chill, slightly later cultivars reduce the risk.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The warmest south-coast zone 10 sites bank under about 300 chill hours most winters, right at or below even Arctic Star's roughly 300-hour requirement. The tree grows and survives easily, but the blossoms drop without setting a reliable crop. Of the cultivars here, none is low-chill enough for dependable fruit.
value.suitability_note_beginner: In the warmest coastal areas, winters are too mild for these nectarine varieties to fruit. The tree will grow happily but give little or no fruit.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest, lowest-chill desert sites bank under about 300 chill hours, below even the lowest-chill cultivar here. The tree survives the heat but the crop does not set. Extreme summer temperatures further stress any fruit that does form.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The hottest desert spots stay too warm in winter for these nectarines to set fruit, and the fierce summer heat works against them too. Expect a living tree but little or no fruit here.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: Low-desert zone 9 banks about 300 to 400 chill hours, so only the lowest-chill nectarine here (Arctic Star at about 300 hours) fits, and only marginally in cooler winters. Plant bare-root in January, choose an early ripener, and expect a crop that finishes before summer heat. Higher-chill cultivars will not fruit.
value.suitability_note_beginner: Only the lowest-chill nectarine varieties can fruit in the Arizona low desert, and even those miss in warm winters. Plant in winter and pick before the summer heat.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: An early bloom can occasionally meet a late desert frost; more often the binding limit is whether the winter banked the 400 chill hours the variety needs.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The cool South Coast (zone 10) banks almost no winter chill (roughly 50 to 350 hours), so sour cherry cannot bloom or set. It will not fruit anywhere on the mild Southern California coast.
value.suitability_note_beginner: The Southern California coast (zone 10) has almost no winter cold, so sour cherry will not fruit at all.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The hottest desert (zone 10) banks essentially no chill (roughly 100 to 300 hours) and its extreme summer heat compounds the problem. Sour cherry is unsuitable.

value.suitability_note_seasoned: The Arizona low desert banks essentially no winter chill (about 100 to 400 hours) and endures extreme summer heat, both hostile to a cold-climate sour cherry. Unsuitable; grow low-chill stone fruit or figs.

value.suitability_note_beginner: Hawaii does not have a cold winter, so sour cherry cannot bloom or fruit here at all. Grow tropical fruit instead.

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Summer gap is a HEAT exclusion, not a frost gap. Celery is a cool-season crop that grows best near 60 to 70°F and suffers above about 75°F: heat coarsens the stalks, turns them bitter, and combined with drought can trigger bolting, so the planting calendar in this region brackets the hottest months and grows celery in the cooler fall, winter, and spring windows. (UC Master Gardeners of Santa Clara County; Utah State University Extension; Texas A&M AgriLife Extension)

value.zone_notes: Zone 9 gives a long harvest and often mild winters, so an established clump frequently overwinters as a perennial; dig or heavily mulch it if a hard freeze threatens.

Zone 10 south coast is near frost-free; an established clump persists as a year-round perennial. Growth slows in the coolest winter weeks, but stalks can be cut in any month. Divide in spring to renew vigor.
Zone 10 low desert is warm and nearly frost-free, giving one of the longest lemongrass seasons; a clump may persist as a perennial. Consistent deep watering is essential in the extreme heat.

Zone 9 low desert (Phoenix, Tucson) gives one of the longest, hottest lemongrass seasons in the country. It loves the heat but demands very heavy watering; irrigate deeply at the base. First frost around November ends the season.

Hawaii's frost-free lowlands support lemongrass as a continuous year-round perennial, harvestable any month. Give it full sun, rich soil, and steady water. Rust (documented on lemongrass in Hawaii) is the main disease; keep clumps open and airy and water at the base to limit it. Divide every few years to renew vigor.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial in name only here, and best grown in a container. The LSU AgCenter is blunt that lavender is a challenge across the humid Gulf South: through the cooler half of the year, roughly October to May, plants grow acceptably, but once summer heat and humidity arrive they trigger root rot, so it is most reliably grown in pots where drainage and air flow can be controlled and the plant moved as seasons change. English lavender largely fails; choose heat- and humidity-tolerant types such as Spanish lavender, Goodwin Creek Grey, or the hybrid Phenomenal. Many growers treat it as a cool-season or short-lived plant. Moderate your expectations.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Lavender is hard to grow in the humid South, so think of it as a container plant for the cooler months. The summer heat and humidity cause root rot, so use a pot with excellent drainage and good airflow, and pick a tough type like Spanish lavender or Phenomenal. Plant in fall and do not expect it to last for years.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Cold is not the problem here; summer heat and humidity are, and they bring root and crown rot. Grow in a well-drained container, keep air moving, water sparingly, and be prepared to replace plants that decline over a humid summer.
value.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=perennial (container-preferred, often short-lived): in the warmer, even more humid Gulf zone 9 lavender is harder still. LSU AgCenter: does well in the milder months but summer heat and humidity bring root rot; grow in containers with excellent drainage. UF/IFAS Panhandle: choose heat- and humidity-tolerant types, not English lavender. bloom is the spring-into-early-summer window, displayed Apr to Jun. plant_out is the fall cool-season window, display-only. resolved_from carries zone 9 frost dates (last Jan 31, first Dec 15) for the deriver. blocks_launch:false open finding: marginal plant, no clean reliably-perennial in-ground T1 bloom window; displayed window reflects cool-season culture and is flagged for community correction.
value.synthesis_note_beginner: In the warm, humid lower Gulf South, lavender is very hard to grow and is best as a container plant for the cool season. Heat and humidity rot it in summer. Plant in fall in a well-drained pot, choose a tough type, and treat it as short-lived. It flowers spring into early summer.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial. The mild southern coast, with hot dry summers and cool wet winters, is an excellent fit for lavender, which lives in the ground as a drought-tolerant woody perennial. Spanish lavender blooms earliest, followed by English lavender and the lavandins. Plant in fall or early spring in full sun and very well-drained soil; overwatering and poor drainage, not cold, are what cause trouble.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Lavender thrives on the mild southern coast and comes back every year. Plant it in fall or early spring in a sunny, fast-draining spot, and do not overwater. It flowers from spring into summer, with Spanish lavender starting early.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Frost is rarely a concern on the southern coast; the real risks are overwatering and poorly drained soil. Keep it lean and dry once established and cut back hard after bloom, not in fall.
value.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=perennial: in the mildest southern-coast pockets (zone 10) lavender is reliably perennial in the ground (UC ANR coastal guidance). bloom runs spring into summer (UC ANR; Spanish earliest), displayed Apr to Jul. plant_out is the fall or early-spring practice (UC IPM), display-only. resolved_from carries zone 10 frost dates (last Jan 15, first Dec 31) from zone_frost_data; this near-frost-free span has the deriver bracket growing across nearly the whole year, correct for the mild coast. Drainage and watering discipline, not cold, are decisive.
value.synthesis_note_beginner: In the mildest southern-coast spots, lavender grows in the ground all year and flowers spring into summer. Plant in fall or early spring and keep it sunny, lean, and fast-draining.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial. Lavender's deep drought tolerance suits the desert, and it lives in the ground for years with sharp drainage, but the intense summer sun is hard on it: give afternoon shade, set plants out in the cool season rather than summer, and expect bloom to finish by early summer as the heat climbs. Spanish lavender and the lavandins tend to take desert heat best.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Lavender can grow in the California desert as a perennial if you plant it in the cool season and give it afternoon shade. Use fast-draining soil and water deeply but seldom. It flowers spring into early summer, then the heat shuts it down.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Heat, not cold, is the limiting factor in the desert. Plant in fall or early spring, give afternoon shade, water deeply but infrequently, and cut back hard after bloom rather than in fall.
value.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=perennial: in the hottest low-desert zone (zone 10) lavender still grows as a drought-tolerant in-ground perennial where drainage is sharp and afternoon shade is provided; dry desert air actually suits it better than humid heat. bloom runs spring into early summer, displayed Apr to Jun, cut short by extreme heat. plant_out is the cool-season fall or early-spring practice (UC IPM), display-only. resolved_from carries zone 10 frost dates (last Jan 15, first Dec 31) from zone_frost_data; this near-frost-free span has the deriver bracket growing across most of the year. Heat and drainage, not cold, are decisive.
value.synthesis_note_beginner: In the hottest low desert, lavender can still be a perennial with afternoon shade and fast-draining soil. It flowers spring into early summer. Plant in the cool season and water deeply but rarely.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Perennial. University of Arizona Extension classes lavender as a perennial for the low desert, planted in the cool season and given frost protection while young. The dry desert air suits it, but the summer sun is brutal: give it morning sun with afternoon shade, sharp drainage, and lean, infrequent water. Spanish lavender does especially well in the low desert. Bloom is a late-spring-to-early-summer flush that the heat brings to an end.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Lavender is a perennial in the Arizona low desert if you plant it in the cool season and shade it from afternoon sun. Use fast-draining soil and water deeply but seldom. Protect young plants from frost. It flowers in late spring to early summer, then the heat slows it down.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: Young plants need protection from the occasional frost, but the bigger challenge is summer heat. Give afternoon shade and sharp drainage, water deeply but infrequently, and cut back hard after bloom rather than in fall.
value.synthesis_note_seasoned: grown_as=perennial: University of Arizona Extension's Tucson herb calendar (az2061) classes lavender as a perennial (P) for the low desert (zone 9) and shows young plants blooming in pots. bloom is a heat-shortened late-spring-to-early-summer flush, displayed May to Jun. plant_out is the cool-season establishment window az2061 gives (October to November and February to April), display-only on this perennial cell; az2061 also flags frost protection for young plants. resolved_from carries zone 9 frost dates (last Jan 31, first Dec 15) for the deriver. Afternoon shade and sharp drainage manage the dominant heat stress; dry desert air otherwise suits lavender well.
value.synthesis_note_beginner: In the Arizona low desert, lavender is a perennial (per University of Arizona Extension) that flowers late spring to early summer. Plant in the cool season, give afternoon shade and fast-draining soil, water sparingly, and protect young plants from frost.

value.grown_as_note_seasoned: Marginal in Hawaii and viable only in cool, dry upcountry microclimates, not in the humid lowlands where most gardening happens. The University of Hawaii CTAHR does not list lavender among its recommended home-garden plants, and CTAHR-extension garden advice classes lavender as an herb for cooler areas and warns against planting it in hot coastal spots without extra pest and disease control. Where it does succeed, as in Kona at higher, drier elevations (roughly 600 to 1,200 ft and up, with hot days and cool nights) and in the upcountry Maui farms, it behaves as a fragrant perennial. If you are not in such a cool, dry microclimate, lavender is not a sound choice; if you are, give it full sun, very sharp drainage, and lean, infrequent water.
value.grown_as_note_beginner: Lavender does not grow well in most of Hawaii because the lowlands are too hot and humid, which rots it. It only does well in cool, dry, higher-elevation places with cool nights, like upcountry Maui or higher parts of Kona. If you live somewhere cool and dry like that, you can grow it as a fragrant perennial in a sunny, fast-draining spot. Otherwise, it is not a good pick.
value.frost_risk_note_seasoned: There is no frost in Hawaii. The real limit is humid lowland heat, which causes rot, so lavender only works in cool, dry, higher-elevation microclimates. There, give it sharp drainage and lean water; at sea level, do not expect success.

value.planting_note: Direct-sow after the last frost once soil is warm (past 50 °F, ideally 70 to 85 °F), about 1 inch deep; first blooms in roughly 60 to 100 days by type, then seed ripens about a month later. Stake tall types, and bag ripening heads to save seed from birds. Sow single-stem cut-flower types again every 1 to 3 weeks through midsummer for a steady supply.

value.notes: A southeastern native, echinacea is well suited here: plant a division or transplant in spring, in full sun and well-drained soil. It blooms from late spring into fall, dies back for a short winter rest, and returns each year. Watch drainage in wet, humid summers to avoid crown rot, deadhead for more bloom or leave cones for the birds, and divide every 3 to 4 years.

On the mild California coast, plant a division or transplant in spring in full sun and well-drained soil. Cooler coastal summers give a summer bloom and a mild, short winter rest; the plant returns each year. Ensure good drainage, keep it lean and on the dry side, deadhead for more bloom or leave the cones for the birds, and divide every few years.

In the desert valleys, plant a division or transplant in late winter into full sun (some afternoon shade helps) and very well-drained soil. Echinacea is heat tolerant and blooms from spring through the warm season; extreme midsummer heat and any wet, poorly drained soil are the stresses to manage. Water deeply but infrequently, keep it lean, and expect a shorter-lived plant here.

In the low desert, echinacea is marginal: it tolerates heat but the extreme summer and any wet soil stress it, so treat it as a shorter-lived plant that blooms mainly from spring into early summer. Set out a division or transplant in late winter in full sun to light afternoon shade and very sharp drainage. Water deeply but infrequently, keep it lean, and be ready to replant. Leave cones for the birds where it does bloom.

Echinacea is a temperate perennial that needs a winter rest, so in the frost-free lowland tropics it is poorly adapted and short-lived, essentially a best-effort planting. If tried, use full sun and very sharp drainage, keep it lean and dry, expect a spring-to-early-fall bloom at best, and plan to replant rather than count on it returning for years. This is the least reliable region for the plant.

value.zone_notes: Zone 9 is the warm limit of reliable bee balm; it blooms in spring into early summer, then struggles in the humid heat. Treat it as marginal, lean on resistant cultivars, and expect powdery mildew pressure to be high.
value.planting_note: Bee balm grows here as a hardy perennial, but the region's heat and humidity make powdery mildew its defining challenge. Set out transplants or divisions in early spring; plants bloom late spring into summer, then rest. Choose mildew-resistant cultivars, space widely for airflow, water at the base, and divide regularly.

value.zone_notes: Zone 10 on the south coast is at the warm, low-chill limit for bee balm; it blooms spring into early summer but is a marginal, short-lived perennial with little winter dormancy. Best grown as a refreshed clump or in containers.
value.planting_note: Bee balm grows here as a perennial in a mild, dry-summer climate; low winter chill makes it a shorter-lived, marginal perennial at the warm end. Set out transplants or divisions in early spring; bloom runs spring into summer. Keep soil moist and divide to keep it vigorous.

value.planting_note: Sweet pea runs as a cool-season, fall-sown crop here: sow in fall (and again in late winter) into deep, rich, well-drained soil, grow it over the mild winter, and cut fragrant stems from late winter into spring. Give a 5 to 6 ft trellis, keep evenly moist, feed moderately, and remove pods to prolong bloom. Summer heat ends the season, so plants are cleared as it warms.

Summer sowing gap is a heat exclusion, not a frost gap: in deep-summer heat cucumber flowering and fruit set falter and the fruit turns bitter. When daytime highs run in the 90s°F and higher with warm nights, heat injures the flowers and pollen so plants set poorly or drop young fruit, and heat-plus-drought stress drives the bitter compound (cucurbitacin) into what fruit does form. Set and quality recover as temperatures ease, which is why these hot regions split into a spring and a fall crop rather than running through summer. (regional extension planting chart; UMN Extension growing cucumbers)

heat_pause.basis_seasoned: Collards tolerate more heat than any other cole crop, but the desert valleys are a genuine extreme: sustained summer highs around and above 105 to 115°F, with germination failing above about 85°F, scorch and stall even collards, so the peak summer is left out of the planting calendar and the crop runs as a fall-through-spring green. The shoulder months can sometimes be pushed with heavy afternoon shade, mulch, and steady water.
